new.title: How Regex::new() works
new.description: Compiles a pattern once, so it can be used many times; a bad pattern is an error.

l1.text: \d = any digit,  + = one or more times

l4.text: a group is opened but never closed

slides.caption: Regex::new() reads the pattern text and builds a matcher from it. This is the slow part, so it is done once.
The pattern \d+ is parsed: \d means one digit, + means one or more of what comes before it.
The pattern is valid, so the compiled matcher comes back as Ok(Regex). Keep it and reuse it: searching with it is fast.
Now "(": a group is started, but there is no ")" to end it.
Regex::new() does not panic on a bad pattern; it returns Err with a message that points at the problem.
r"\d+" → Ok, "(" → Err. Write patterns as raw strings (r"...") so the backslashes reach the regex unchanged.

is-match.title: How Regex::is_match() works
is-match.description: Says whether the pattern matches anywhere in the text.

note.text: re = Regex::new(r"\d+"): one or more digits

slides.caption: is_match() looks for the pattern anywhere in the text. It only answers yes or no.
a, b and c are not digits, so no match starts there.
At 1 a digit is found, so the pattern matches. is_match() can stop right here: it does not need to know where the match ends.
The pattern matches anywhere in the text unless it is anchored: r"^\d+$" would need the whole text to be digits, and "abc123" would give false.
re.is_match("abc123") is true. Use find() when you also need where the match is.

find.title: How Regex::find() works
find.description: Gives the first, leftmost match and where it is.

slides.caption: find() returns the first match, as an Option<Match> with the matched text and its byte positions.
The search starts at the left. a and b are not digits.
At index 2 a digit starts a match. + is greedy: it takes as many digits as it can, so it takes 2 as well.
c is not a digit, so the match ends before index 4. The match is "12", from 2 up to (not including) 4.
find() stops after the first match. "345" is also a match, but it is not looked at.
find() returns Some(Match) with as_str() = "12", start() = 2 and end() = 4. Use find_iter() for every match.

find-iter.title: How Regex::find_iter() works
find-iter.description: Yields every match, left to right, without overlaps.

slides.caption: find_iter() repeats the search: after each match it continues from where that match ended.
The first match is "12" at 2..4.
The search goes on from index 4. c and d are skipped.
The next match is "345" at 6..9. Matches never overlap, because each search starts after the previous match.
The end of the text is reached, so the iterator ends.
Collected with .map(|m| m.as_str()), the matches are "12" and "345".

captures.title: How Regex::captures() works
captures.description: Finds a match and gives the parts matched by each group in ( ).

slides.caption: Each ( ) in the pattern is a capture group. captures() returns the whole match and what every group matched.
Group 1, the first (\d+), matches the digits 10.
The - in the pattern matches the - in the text. It is not inside a group, so it is not captured on its own.
Group 2, the second (\d+), matches 20.
Group 0 is always the whole match: "10-20".
caps[1] is "10" and caps[2] is "20" (indexing panics if a group did not match; caps.get(1) returns an Option).

captures-name.title: How Captures::name() works
captures-name.description: Gets a capture group by its name instead of its number.

slides.caption: (?P<year>...) gives a group a name. \d{4} means exactly 4 digits, \d{2} exactly 2.
The group named year matches the first 4 digits.
The - matches, then the group named month matches 2 digits.
caps.name("year") looks the group up by name and returns Some(Match). Names keep code readable when groups are added or moved.
caps.name("year") is Some("2024") and caps.name("month") is Some("03"). An unknown name gives None.

captures-iter.title: How Regex::captures_iter() works
captures-iter.description: Gives the capture groups of every match.

slides.caption: captures_iter() is find_iter() with groups: for each match it yields a Captures. \w+ is one or more letters, digits or _.
First match: group 1 is "a", group 2 is "1".
The space does not match, so the search moves on.
Second match: group 1 is "b", group 2 is "22".
Mapped with |c| (c[1].to_string(), c[2].to_string()), the matches give ("a", "1") and ("b", "22"). Parse the numbers with .parse() if you need integers.
replace() finds the first match and puts the replacement in its place.
The first match is the digit 1.
It is replaced by "#".
replace() stops after one replacement: the 2 is also a digit, but it stays.
replace() returns "a#b2" as a Cow<str>: if nothing matches, the original text is returned without copying. Use replace_all() for every match.

replace-all.title: How Regex::replace_all() works
replace-all.description: Replaces every match; $1, $2 insert the groups.

slides.caption: replace_all() replaces every match. In the replacement, $1 and $2 stand for what group 1 and group 2 matched.
The match "10-20" has group 1 = "10" and group 2 = "20".
The replacement "$2-$1" becomes "20" + "-" + "10".
There are no more matches, so the result is complete. With more matches, each would be swapped the same way.
replace_all("10-20", "$2-$1") gives "20-10". Write ${1}x when a letter follows a group number, or $1x is read as a group named 1x.

split.title: How Regex::split() works
split.description: Cuts the text at every match of the pattern.

note.text: re = Regex::new(r"[,;]"): a comma or a semicolon

slides.caption: split() uses the matches as separators and yields the text between them. [,;] matches one character that is , or ;.
The first separator is the comma. The text before it, "a", is yielded.
The next separator is the semicolon: "b" is yielded.
After the last separator comes "c". The separators themselves are not part of the result.
split() yields "a", "b", "c". str::split can only split on fixed text; a regex can split on several kinds of separators at once.

splitn.title: How Regex::splitn() works
splitn.description: Splits into at most n pieces; the last piece keeps the rest.

slides.caption: splitn(text, 2) splits like split(), but stops when it has 2 pieces.
The first comma splits off "a". That is piece 1.
Piece 2 is the last one allowed, so it is everything that is left, commas included.
The other commas are not used as separators.
splitn(.., 2) gives "a" and "b,c,d". Useful for "key=value=more" when only the first = separates the key.

escape.title: How regex::escape() works
escape.description: Makes text match literally by escaping the characters that have a meaning in patterns.

note.text: + means "one or more" in a pattern

slides.caption: In a pattern, + is an operator. To search for the text "1+1=2" itself, the + must be escaped.
escape() checks every character. 1 is a plain character: unchanged.
+ has a meaning in patterns, so a backslash is put in front of it: \+.
1, = and 2 are plain characters.
escape() returns "1\+1=2". Regex::new(&regex::escape(text)) matches exactly that text. Without escaping, "1+1=2" would match "11=2" or "111=2".

regex-set-matches.title: How RegexSet::matches() works
regex-set-matches.description: Tests many patterns against a text in one pass.

slides.caption: A RegexSet compiles several patterns together. matches() scans the text once and reports which patterns match somewhere.
Pattern 0, \d, matches the 1 in "a1".
Pattern 1, [a-z], matches the a.
Pattern 2, !, matches nowhere: there is no ! in "a1".
matches() returns a SetMatches holding the indices 0 and 1. It does not say where each match is; use the separate Regex for that.
set.matches("a1").into_iter() yields 0, 1. Handy for routing: one scan tells which of many rules apply.
